title: I. Father Ferapont
paragraphs: Alyosha was woken early, before daybreak. Father Zossima had woken feeling very weak, yet he wanted to get out of bed and sit in a chair. His mind was perfectly clear. His face looked worn out, but it was bright and almost joyful, full of gaiety, kindness and warmth. “Perhaps I will not live through the coming day,” he told Alyosha. Then he asked to confess and take communion at once. He always confessed to Father Païssy. After communion came the service of extreme unction. The monks gathered, and little by little the cell filled with the residents of the hermitage. By now it was daylight. People began to arrive from the monastery. When the service was over, the elder wanted to kiss every one of them and say goodbye. The cell was so small that the first visitors left to make room for the next. Alyosha stood beside the elder, who was seated in his armchair again. He talked as much as he could. His voice was weak, but fairly steady.

“I have been teaching you for so many years, and so I have been talking aloud for so many years, that talking has become a habit. It is almost harder for me to keep quiet than to speak, even now, weak as I am, dear Fathers and brothers,” he joked, looking with emotion at the group around him.

Alyosha remembered some of what he said, afterwards. The elder spoke out clearly and his voice was fairly steady, but what he said hung together rather loosely. He spoke of many things. He seemed anxious, before the moment of death, to say everything he had not said in his life. It was not only to instruct them. He seemed thirsty to share his joy and ecstasy with all men and all creation, and to open his whole heart once more in his life.

“Love one another, Fathers,” said Father Zossima, as far as Alyosha could remember afterwards. “Love God’s people. We have come here and shut ourselves up within these walls, but we are no holier than those outside. On the contrary, by the very act of coming here, each of us has admitted to himself that he is worse than others, worse than all men on earth.... And the longer a monk lives in seclusion, the more keenly he must see this. Otherwise he would have had no reason to come. When he understands that he is not only worse than others, but that he is responsible to all men for all and everything, for all human sins, national and individual, only then is the aim of our seclusion reached. For know, dear ones, that every one of us is undoubtedly responsible for all men and everything on earth. This is not merely because creation as a whole is sinful. Each one of us is personally responsible for all mankind and for every single man. This knowledge is the crown of life for the monk and for every man. For monks are not a special sort of men, but only what all men ought to be. Only through that knowledge does our heart grow soft with infinite, universal, inexhaustible love. Then each of you will have the power to win over the whole world by love and to wash away the sins of the world with your tears.... Each of you, keep watch over your heart and confess your sins to yourself without ceasing. Do not be afraid of your sins, even when you see them, so long as there is penitence. But do not make conditions with God. Again I say, do not be proud. Do not be proud before the little or before the great. Do not hate those who reject you, who insult you, who abuse and slander you. Do not hate the atheists, the teachers of evil, the materialists—and I mean not only the good ones—for there are many good ones among them, especially in our day—do not hate even the wicked ones. Remember them in your prayers in this way: Save, O Lord, all those who have no one to pray for them, save also all those who will not pray. And add: it is not in pride that I make this prayer, O Lord, for I am lower than all men.... Love God’s people. Do not let strangers draw away the flock, for if you sleep in your slothfulness and disdainful pride, or worse still, in covetousness, they will come from every side and draw your flock away. Expound the Gospel to the people unceasingly ... do not be extortionate.... Do not love gold and silver, do not hoard them.... Have faith. Cling to the banner and raise it on high.”

But the elder actually spoke more disconnectedly than Alyosha made it seem when he reported the words afterwards. Now and then he stopped altogether, as if to draw breath and gather strength, yet he was in a kind of ecstasy. They listened with emotion, though many were puzzled by his words and found them obscure.... Afterwards everyone remembered them.

Alyosha stepped out of the cell for a moment and was struck by the excitement and suspense of the monks crowding around it. In some, this expectation took the form of anxiety; in others, of devout solemnity. All of them expected some marvel to happen right after the elder’s death. Seen from one side, their suspense was almost frivolous, yet even the strictest of the monks were caught up in it. Father Païssy’s face was the gravest of all.

A monk called Alyosha aside, secretly, to see Rakitin. Rakitin had come from town with a singular letter for him from Madame Hohlakov. In it she described a strange and very timely incident. Among the women who had come the day before to receive Father Zossima’s blessing, it seemed, was an old woman from the town, a sergeant’s widow named Prohorovna. She had asked whether she might pray for the repose of the soul of her son Vassenka, who had gone to Irkutsk and had sent her no word for over a year. Father Zossima had answered her sternly and forbidden it. Praying for the living as though they were dead, he said, was a kind of sorcery. Later he forgave her, because she was ignorant, and added some words of comfort, “as though reading the book of the future” (this was Madame Hohlakov’s expression): “that her son Vassya was certainly alive and would either come himself very soon or send a letter, and that she should go home and expect him.” And then Madame Hohlakov exclaimed enthusiastically, “Would you believe it? The prophecy has come true to the letter, and more besides.” The old woman had barely got home when they handed her a letter from Siberia that had been waiting for her. But that was not all. In the letter, written on the road from Ekaterinenburg, Vassya told his mother that he was coming back to Russia with an official, and that three weeks after she got the letter he hoped “to embrace his mother.”

Madame Hohlakov warmly begged Alyosha to tell the Superior and the whole brotherhood about this new “miracle of prediction.” “All, all, ought to know of it!” she finished. The letter had been written in a hurry, and the writer’s excitement showed in every line. But Alyosha did not need to tell the monks, because they all knew already. Rakitin had told the monk who carried his message “to inform most respectfully his reverence Father Païssy that he, Rakitin, has a matter to speak of with him, so grave that he dare not put it off a moment, and humbly begs forgiveness for his presumption.” That monk had delivered the message to Father Païssy before delivering Alyosha’s. So when Alyosha had read the letter, he found nothing left to do but hand it to Father Païssy as confirmation of the story.
Even that austere and cautious man frowned as he read the news of the “miracle,” yet he could not entirely hide some inner emotion. His eyes gleamed, and a grave, solemn smile came to his lips.
“We shall see greater things!” broke from him.
“We shall see greater things, greater things yet!” the monks around him echoed.

But Father Païssy frowned again and asked them all, for a time at least, not to speak of the matter “until it is more fully confirmed, since there is so much credulity among those of this world, and besides, this may well have come about naturally.” He added this prudently, as if to ease his conscience, though he hardly believed his own disclaimer. His listeners saw that perfectly well.

Within the hour, of course, the whole monastery knew of the “miracle,” and so did many visitors who had come for the mass. No one seemed more struck by it than the monk who had come the day before from St. Sylvester, from the little monastery of Obdorsk in the far North. He had stood near Madame Hohlakov the previous day and had earnestly asked Father Zossima, referring to the “healing” of the lady’s daughter, “How can you presume to do such things?”

Now he was rather puzzled and did not know whom to believe. The evening before, he had visited Father Ferapont in his separate cell behind the apiary, and the visit had left him deeply impressed and awed. This Father Ferapont was the aged monk, devoted to fasting and silence, who has been mentioned already as opposed to Father Zossima and to the whole institution of “elders,” which he held to be a harmful and frivolous novelty. He was a formidable opponent, although his practice of silence meant he hardly spoke to anyone. He was formidable because a number of monks shared his feelings entirely, and many visitors saw him as a great saint and ascetic, even though they had no doubt he was crazy. Yet it was precisely his craziness that drew them.

Father Ferapont never went to see the elder. He lived in the hermitage, but nobody bothered him to follow its rules, and this too was because he acted as if he were crazy. He was seventy-five or older. His home was in a corner beyond the apiary, an old, decaying wooden cell built long ago for another great ascetic, Father Iona, who had lived to a hundred and five. Many curious stories about his saintly deeds were still told in the monastery and the neighborhood.

Seven years earlier, Father Ferapont had succeeded in getting himself settled in that same lonely cell. It was just a peasant’s hut, though it looked like a chapel, because it held an extraordinary number of ikons with lamps burning before them without a break—ikons that people had brought to the monastery as offerings to God. Father Ferapont had been appointed to look after them and keep the lamps lit. It was said (and it was true) that he ate only two pounds of bread in three days. The beekeeper, who lived close to the apiary, brought him the bread every three days, and even to this man who served him, Father Ferapont seldom spoke a word. These four pounds of bread, plus the sacrament bread that the Father Superior regularly sent him on Sundays after the late mass, made up his weekly food. The water in his jug was changed every day. He seldom showed himself at mass. Visitors who came to pay him homage sometimes found him kneeling in prayer all day without once looking around. When he did speak to them, he was brief, abrupt, odd, and nearly always rude. Very rarely, though, he would talk with visitors. Mostly he would come out with a single strange saying that was a complete riddle, and no pleading could make him say a word to explain it. He was not a priest, but a simple monk. There was a strange belief, mainly among the most ignorant, that Father Ferapont communicated with heavenly spirits and spoke only with them, which was why he was silent with men.

The beekeeper, who was also a very silent and surly monk, had pointed the monk from Obdorsk toward the apiary, and he made his way to the corner where Father Ferapont’s cell stood. “Maybe he will speak, since you are a stranger, and maybe you will get nothing out of him,” the beekeeper had warned. The monk said afterwards that he approached in utter dread. It was rather late in the evening. Father Ferapont was sitting at the door of his cell on a low bench. A huge old elm rustled gently overhead. There was a freshness in the evening air. The monk from Obdorsk bowed low before the saint and asked for his blessing.
“Do you want me to bow down to you, monk?” said Father Ferapont. “Get up!”
The monk got to his feet.
“Blessing, be blessed! Sit down next to me. Where have you come from?”

What startled the poor monk most was that Father Ferapont, for all his strict fasting and his great age, still looked like a vigorous old man. He was tall and stood perfectly straight. His face was thin, yet fresh and healthy. He plainly still had a good deal of strength, and his build was that of an athlete. He was very old, but his hair was thick and his beard full, and neither was even fully gray. Both had once been black. His eyes were large, gray and bright, though they stood out strikingly from his face. He had a broad country accent. He wore a peasant’s long reddish coat made of coarse convict cloth (as it used to be called), tied round the waist with a stout rope. His throat and chest were bare. Under the coat, his shirt of the coarsest linen was almost black with dirt, for it had not been changed in months. People said he wore thirty pounds of iron chains beneath the coat. On his bare feet were old slippers that were nearly falling apart.
“From the little Obdorsk monastery, from St. Sylvester,” the monk answered humbly. All the while his keen, curious, slightly frightened little eyes were watching the hermit.
“I’ve been to your Sylvester’s. I used to stay there. Is Sylvester well?”
The monk hesitated.
“What a senseless lot you are! How do you keep the fasts?”

“We eat according to the ancient rules of the monastery. In Lent no meals are provided on Monday, Wednesday and Friday. On Tuesday and Thursday we are given white bread, stewed fruit with honey, wild berries or salted cabbage, and porridge of coarse meal. On Saturday there is white cabbage soup, noodles with peas, and kasha, all of it made with hemp oil. On weekdays we get dried fish and kasha along with the cabbage soup. In Holy Week, from Monday to Saturday evening, six whole days, nothing at all is cooked. We have only bread and water, and little of that, and if possible we do not eat every day, as is ordered for the first week of Lent. On Good Friday we eat nothing. On the Saturday, too, we must fast until three o’clock, and then we take a little bread and water and drink one cup of wine. On Holy Thursday we drink wine and have something cooked without oil, or nothing cooked at all, because the council of Laodicea says of Holy Thursday: ‘It is unseemly to relax the fast on Holy Thursday and so dishonor the whole of Lent!’ That is how we keep the fast. But what is that beside you, holy Father,” added the monk, growing more confident, “who take nothing but bread and water all year round, even at Easter? What we eat in two days lasts you a full seven. Your great abstinence is truly marvelous.”
“And mushrooms?” Father Ferapont asked suddenly.
“Mushrooms?” the monk repeated, taken aback.

“Yes. I can do without their bread. I don’t need it at all. I can go off into the forest and live on mushrooms or berries. But they can’t do without their bread here, and that’s why they’re in bondage to the devil. These days the unclean say there’s no need for such fasting. Proud and unclean is their judgment.”
“Och, true,” sighed the monk.
“And have you seen devils among them?” Ferapont asked.
“Among them? Among whom?” the monk asked timidly.

“Last year on Trinity Sunday I went to see the Father Superior, and I haven’t been back since. I saw a devil sitting on one man’s chest, hiding under his cassock, only his horns sticking out. Another had one peeping out of his pocket, with sharp eyes, and it was afraid of me. Another had settled in somebody’s unclean belly. Another was hanging round a man’s neck, and the man was carrying him about without seeing him.”
“You—you can see spirits?” the monk asked.

“I tell you, I can see. I see right through them. When I came out from the Superior’s, I saw one hiding from me behind the door. A big one, a yard and a half high or more, with a thick long gray tail. The tip of the tail was in the crack of the door, and I was quick. I slammed the door and pinched his tail in it. He squealed and began to struggle. I made the sign of the cross over him three times, and he died on the spot, like a crushed spider. He must be rotting there in the corner and stinking by now, but they don’t see it, they don’t smell it. It’s a year since I was there. I’m telling you this because you’re a stranger.”

“Your words are terrible! But, holy and blessed Father,” said the monk, who was getting bolder and bolder, “is it true what people say about you, even in far-off lands, that you are in constant communication with the Holy Ghost?”
“He does fly down sometimes.”
“How does he fly down? In what form?”
“As a bird.”
“The Holy Ghost as a dove?”
“There’s the Holy Ghost, and there’s the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit can appear as other birds. Sometimes as a swallow, sometimes as a goldfinch, sometimes as a blue-tit.”
“How can you tell him from an ordinary tit?”
“He talks.”
“How does he talk? In what language?”
“Human language.”
“And what does he say to you?”
“Why, today he told me a fool would come to see me and ask me improper questions. You want to know too much, monk.”
“Your words are terrible, most holy and blessed Father,” the monk said, shaking his head. Yet there was doubt in his frightened little eyes.
“See this tree?” Father Ferapont asked, after a pause.
“I see it, blessed Father.”
“You think it’s an elm. To me it’s a different shape.”
“What shape?” asked the monk, after waiting in vain for him to go on.
“It happens at night. Do you see those two branches? At night it is Christ stretching out His arms to me, searching for me with those arms. I see it plainly, and I tremble. It’s terrible, terrible!”
“What’s terrible about it, if it is Christ Himself?”
“Why, He’ll seize me and carry me off.”
“Alive?”
“In the spirit and glory of Elijah, haven’t you heard? He’ll take me up in His arms and carry me away.”

The monk went back to the cell he was sharing with one of the brothers, and he was greatly perplexed. Even so, in his heart he revered Father Ferapont more than Father Zossima. He was all in favor of fasting, so it did not seem strange to him that a man who kept such a rigid fast as Father Ferapont should “see marvels.” His words certainly sounded queer, but only God could say what lay hidden in them. And were worse words and deeds not commonly seen in people who have given up their minds for the glory of God? The tale of the devil’s tail caught in the door he was ready and eager to believe, and not only as a figure of speech. Besides, before coming to the monastery he had been strongly prejudiced against the institution of “elders.” He knew it only from hearsay and thought it a harmful novelty. He had not been at the monastery long before he noticed the secret grumbling of some shallow brothers who disliked it. He was, besides, a meddlesome, curious man who poked his nose into everything. That was why the news of the fresh “miracle” performed by Father Zossima left him so deeply perplexed. Alyosha remembered afterwards how their inquisitive guest from Obdorsk kept flitting from one group to another, listening and asking questions among the monks crowded inside and outside the elder’s cell. At the time, though, he paid him little attention, and only recalled it later.

In fact, he had no thought to spare for it. Father Zossima had grown tired again and gone back to bed. As he was closing his eyes, he thought of Alyosha and sent for him. Alyosha ran to him at once. No one else was in the cell except Father Païssy, Father Iosif and the novice Porfiry. The elder opened his weary eyes, looked hard at Alyosha, and suddenly asked him:
“Are your people expecting you, my son?”
Alyosha hesitated.
“Do they not need you? Did you not promise someone yesterday that you would visit them today?”
“I did promise—my father—my brothers—others too.”

“You see, you must go. Do not grieve. Be sure that I will not die without your being here to hear my last word. I will say that word to you, my son. It will be my last gift to you. To you, dear son, because you love me. But now go and keep your promise.”

Alyosha obeyed at once, though it was hard to leave. But the promise that he would hear the elder’s last word on earth, and that it would be his own last gift to him, filled Alyosha’s soul with a thrill of rapture. He hurried so that he could finish what he had to do in the town and come back quickly. Father Païssy, as they left the cell together, also spoke some words of exhortation that moved and greatly surprised him.

“Remember always, young man,” Father Païssy began, without any preface, “that the science of this world has grown into a great power. In the last century especially, it has analyzed everything divine that has come down to us in the holy books. After that cruel analysis, the learned men of this world have nothing left of all that was once sacred. But they have analyzed only the parts and missed the whole, and their blindness is truly marvelous. The whole still stands firm before their eyes, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. Has it not lasted nineteen centuries? Is it not still a living, moving power in the soul of the individual and in the masses of the people? It is just as strong and alive even in the souls of atheists, who have destroyed everything! Even those who have renounced Christianity and attack it still follow the Christian ideal in their inmost being. Until now neither their cleverness nor the ardor of their hearts has been able to create a higher ideal of man and of virtue than the one Christ gave long ago. When they have tried, the result has been only grotesque. Remember this above all, young man, because your dying elder is sending you out into the world. Perhaps, when you remember this great day, you will not forget my words. They come from my heart, for your guidance, since you are young, and the temptations of the world are great, beyond your strength to bear. Well, now go, my orphan.”

With these words Father Païssy blessed him. As Alyosha left the monastery and turned them over in his mind, he suddenly saw that he had found a new and unexpected friend, a warmly loving teacher, in this austere monk who until now had been stern with him. It was as if Father Zossima had left him to Father Païssy at his death. “Perhaps that is exactly what passed between them,” Alyosha thought suddenly. The philosophical reflections he had just heard so unexpectedly showed how warm Father Païssy’s heart was. He was in a hurry to arm the boy’s mind for the struggle with temptation, and to protect the young soul left in his care with the strongest defense he could think of.
